strengths: The paper addresses a practically useful problem: region- and palette-controlled sketch colourisation with explicit spatial control, which is valuable for design workflows where text prompts are too ambiguous.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually sensible: global sketch-to-image generation provides plausible texture/appearance, while local composition plus inversion and attention injection aims to preserve user-specified colours and smooth boundaries.

The manuscript evaluates across multiple domains, including AFHQ, Places365, Danbooru, and Pascal VOC, and includes comparisons to several recent sketch/image colourisation and reference-based methods.
The qualitative results are often visually convincing, especially for local colour placement and boundary harmonisation compared with naive text- or reference-guided baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations on palette size, attention injection variants, exceptional prompt inversion, SDEdit-style refinement, and the tau tradeoff, which helps explain some design choices.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited. Much of the system is an engineering composition of existing components, including Stable Diffusion v1.5, Scribble ControlNet, BLIP-2, CSS colour-name lookup, DPM-Solver++ inversion, TF-ICON-style exceptional prompts, and Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention injection. The paper presents this as several “firsts,” but the technical advance over prior training-free composition/editing methods is not sharply isolated.

Some quantitative claims are not supported by the reported tables. For example, the text claims the proposed method obtains the best FID and DCCW across all local-colourisation datasets, but Table 1 shows ColorFlow has much better FID on Danbooru2023 than the proposed method, and several PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS values are worse than competitors. This undermines confidence in the interpretation of results.

The evaluation protocol is questionable for a generative colourisation task. Metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS against a single ground-truth image are weak indicators when many valid colourisations exist. The method is also given dominant colours extracted from ground truth images in several experiments, making the setup partly reconstruction-like and not fully representative of user-specified creative palettes.

The fairness of baseline comparisons is unclear. For local colourisation, baselines receive reference patches while the proposed method extracts dominant colours and uses a two-stage pipeline; for global colourisation, IDeepColor uses sampled hints from ground truth. The paper does not sufficiently justify that all methods receive equivalent information or comparable tuning effort.

The claimed efficiency is overstated. Although individual sampling may use 15-20 steps, the full method requires multiple global generations for n palettes plus an auxiliary image, ODE inversion, and final refinement. Runtime scaling with the number of regions, memory use, and wall-clock comparisons are not reported.

The method still depends on manually supplied region masks, often via Photoshop. This is acceptable as an interface choice, but the paper’s claims about convenience should be tempered because mask creation can be a significant burden for complex sketches.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact prompts, seed handling, mask-generation protocol, baseline settings, number of sampled variants/manual selections, and implementation details for attention injection are insufficiently specified for reliable replication.

There are technical ambiguities and apparent formulation issues, such as the definition of the combined mask using max rather than an operation that clips at 1, and vague descriptions of how self-attention maps are injected across layers/timesteps. These may be presentation errors, but they affect technical clarity.

No user study is provided despite the paper being framed around designer workflow and controllability. Human preference or task-completion evaluation would be more appropriate than relying mostly on automated metrics and selected qualitative examples.

The paper contains several writing and formatting problems, including awkward claims, noisy equation rendering, and occasional overstatement. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they add friction and make some technical details harder to verify.

strengths: The paper targets a useful and practical interaction model for sketch colourisation: sketches plus region masks plus color palettes. This is a relevant problem for creative workflows, and the proposed interface is more spatially precise than pure text prompting.

The two-stage design is sensible at a high level. Using a global sketch-to-image stage followed by local composition/refinement can plausibly separate semantic realism from user-specified regional control.

The manuscript includes comparisons across several domains and reports both global and local colourisation tables, plus ablations for palette size, attention injection, exceptional prompt inversion, and the scaling factor tau.

Qualitative examples suggest the pipeline can generate visually appealing results in some cases, especially when the input masks are large and the desired colours align with what the pretrained diffusion model can render.
weaknesses: The contribution is mostly an assembly of existing components: BLIP-2 for class prediction, CSS3/K-D tree color-name lookup, Scribble ControlNet/SD for generation, DPM-Solver++ inversion, TF-ICON-like exceptional prompts, and Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention injection. The paper repeatedly calls parts novel or custom, but the technical novelty beyond system integration is limited and not sharply isolated.

The empirical evidence does not convincingly support the strong claims. In local colourisation, the proposed method is not consistently best on LPIPS, PSNR, or SSIM; for Danbooru2023 and PascalVOC2012 several baselines outperform it on these metrics. In global colourisation, the proposed method often improves FID/LPIPS/SSIM but is worse than T2I-Adapter+IDeepColor on DCCW in multiple datasets, which directly concerns colour fidelity.

The comparisons are potentially unfair or at least not cleanly aligned. Local baselines receive reference patches while the proposed method extracts dominant colours and uses masks/palettes; global comparisons include a stronger Anime-Painter/CounterfeitXL backbone for the proposed method on Danbooru, which makes it hard to attribute gains to the proposed algorithm rather than the pretrained model choice.

The evaluation setup is weak for the claimed professional design workflow. Most sketches are synthetic edge maps from image datasets, palettes are extracted from ground-truth images, and local masks are random. This does not test the intended setting of human-created sketch regions and deliberate designer palettes. The in-the-wild evaluation is only 15 qualitative examples from Freepik and no user study is provided.

Several claims are overstated. The paper says mask count has no impact on quality, but evaluates only two random masks and the method requires generating separate global results per palette/region, so computational cost clearly scales with the number of regions. The claimed 15-20 step efficiency is also incomplete because the full pipeline includes multiple global generations, inversion, and final sampling.

Important technical details are underspecified for reproducibility: exact prompts and negative prompts are only partially described, mask construction for the benchmark is vague, random seed/variant selection is unclear, BLIP-2 VQA prompting and failure handling are not fully specified, and there is no evidence of code release or runtime breakdown for the full multi-region pipeline.

The quantitative metrics are not fully appropriate for the task. Pixel-level PSNR/SSIM against ground truth are of limited meaning for stochastic colourisation, while FID over relatively small or mixed subsets may not reflect region-level controllability. The paper lacks direct measurements of mask-region color accuracy, boundary bleeding, sketch-line preservation, or user preference, which are central to the stated contribution.

The ablations are mostly qualitative and do not isolate the proposed components rigorously. For example, attention injection variants are shown in small figures without quantitative support, and the benefit of exceptional prompts is asserted from limited visual evidence.

Clarity is uneven. The method section contains notation and wording issues, such as referring to the self-attention output as a map, ambiguous timestep intervals for tau, and imprecise statements like local mask count not affecting quality. The paper also contains formatting/grammar problems and very strong promotional language that is not matched by the evidence.

The limitations section acknowledges small-region color fidelity and CSS3 color-name constraints, but does not engage with larger limitations such as dependence on pretrained model priors, failure under incorrect BLIP class predictions, inability to guarantee exact hex-code reproduction, and possible manual effort required to create clean masks.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically meaningful problem: precise, region-aware sketch colourisation from masks and palettes. This input interface is well motivated for design workflows and is more controllable than purely text-guided sketch-to-image generation.

The proposed two-stage training-free pipeline is technically coherent. It combines global ControlNet-based sketch colourisation, palette-to-colour-name conversion, pixel/latent composition, DPM-Solver++ inversion, noise incorporation, and self-attention injection in a way that directly addresses local colour fidelity and boundary harmonisation.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering AFHQ, Places, Danbooru2023, PascalVOC2012, and in-the-wild sketches, with separate global and local comparisons against relevant baselines. The tables show consistent gains in FID and DCCW in several settings, and the qualitative figures support the claim that the method often yields vivid, coherent, locally controlled results.

The ablations are useful and targeted: palette size, attention-map injection choices, exceptional-prompt inversion, and the scaling factor tau are each examined, giving reasonable evidence that the main design components matter.

The training-free nature and compatibility with stronger pretrained backbones are useful contributions. The method may be attractive to practitioners because it can exploit existing diffusion models without collecting task-specific training data.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than high. Many ingredients are borrowed from existing systems, including Scribble ControlNet, BLIP-2, CSS colour naming, DPM-Solver++ inversion, TF-ICON-style exceptional prompts, and Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention control. The contribution is mainly the task formulation and integration pipeline, not a fundamentally new model or learning principle.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. For local colourisation, the proposed method is not uniformly best across LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM; on Danbooru2023 and PascalVOC2012, several baselines outperform it on multiple reconstruction metrics. The paper emphasizes FID and DCCW to support superiority, but the mixed metric picture should be discussed more carefully.

The evaluation protocol is partly synthetic and may not fully reflect real user workflows. Sketches are generated from real images using edge detectors, palettes are extracted from ground truth, and local experiments use two random masks. This does not fully test manually drawn sketches, real artist masks, difficult small regions, overlapping masks, or palette choices that intentionally deviate from the source image.

The local-control comparison has fairness ambiguities. Baselines receive reference patches while the proposed method extracts dominant colours and uses a two-stage diffusion pipeline; this may compare different forms of conditioning. A clearer protocol or additional comparisons to mask-conditioned/inpainting baselines would make the evidence stronger.

Efficiency and reproducibility are under-specified. The paper states 15-20 inference steps and consumer-GPU feasibility, but the full pipeline requires multiple global generations for n palettes, an auxiliary image, inversion, and refinement. End-to-end runtime, memory use, random seed sensitivity, and exact prompt/mask-generation details are not reported sufficiently for a complete reproducibility assessment.

The method has plausible failure modes that are only lightly covered: small selected regions may lose colour fidelity, CSS3 colour names limit chromatic precision, BLIP-2 class prediction can fail on abstract sketches, and the dependence on pretrained generative priors may hallucinate texture or semantics beyond the sketch. These limitations do not undermine acceptance, but they constrain the strength of the contribution.
